source_review.notes: Checked all fourteen references. Current namespace, multi-tenancy, RBAC escalation, Pod Security, network-policy, and checklist guidance was checked against official Kubernetes documentation. Account/organization/landing-zone boundaries were checked against current AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud guidance. Container and hardening claims were checked against NIST and CISA/NSA sources. Provider-specific claims remain explicitly qualified.

evidence: Reviewed workload placement tuple, boundary set, shared-surface/control functions, sufficiency obligation, blast-radius set, and fleet drift set.
Confirmed tuple, set, function, cardinality, implication, model, inequality, union-condition, and subscript notation is defined and GitHub-renderable.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Notation keeps organizational, account, cluster, namespace, runtime, data, key, failure, and evidence boundaries separate.

evidence: Executed all ten placement observations and reproduced conforming=5 plus one each account_gap, cluster_gap, runtime_gap, network_gap, and stale_evidence.
Verified evidence ages 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 satisfy the 12-hour threshold while age 25 does not.
Checked the mutually exclusive first-failure classification totals ten observations.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The synthetic predicate illustrates layered classification; it does not test live provider or Kubernetes controls.

evidence: Verified adding a namespace boundary removes neither shared node/control-plane surfaces nor account, network, data, key, operator, and provider dependencies.
Verified distinct clusters remove selected Kubernetes shared surfaces but do not imply distinct management authority when account credentials and fleet agents remain shared.
Verified zero drift cannot be inferred from observed equality if fleet inventory is incomplete or evidence freshness is unbounded.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: Boundary nesting is treated as a composition of scoped controls rather than monotonic proof of complete isolation.

evidence: Reviewed RBAC bind/escalate/impersonate/token/pod paths, cluster-scoped resources, privileged workload/node escape, webhook/CRD compromise, label manipulation, unsupported network policy, metadata, and public API exposure.
Reviewed account owner, organization admin, cross-account roles, transit/DNS, shared registry/secrets/logging/fleet credentials, provider and organization quota, and stale fleet evidence.

Reviewed node/control-plane/account loss, admission outage, bad rollout/rollback, backup target mismatch, migration dual authority, external-resource orphaning, cluster/account closure, and identifier reuse.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Coverage spans API, runtime, management, identity, network, data, capacity, fleet, recovery, and disposal surfaces.

evidence: Traced resource scope and escalation restraint through namespace vending, RBAC, admission, service accounts, pod/runtime placement, cluster extensions, and self-service APIs.
Traced connectivity and data/key boundaries through network policy, cloud transit, shared services, workload identity, provider resources, and restore.
Traced fleet and lifecycle invariants through desired state, evidence freshness, rings, capacity, migration fencing, provider reconciliation, and decommission.
invariant_checking.notes: No infrastructure container is allowed to imply protection outside the surfaces it actually controls.

evidence: Reviewed two distinct clusters that retain a shared cloud account, administrator credential, transit network, quota domain, and global cluster-admin fleet agent.
Confirmed compromise or destructive action through a shared management surface can affect both clusters.
Confirmed separate clusters still constrain cluster-control-plane hazards without proving separate total management authority.
proof_review.notes: The counterexample correctly refutes only the overbroad implication while preserving valid scoped benefits.

evidence: The separate-cluster management-authority counterexample is explicitly labeled a proof sketch.
Its premises, remaining shared surfaces, counterexample consequence, and bounded conclusion are stated.
Sufficiency, blast-radius, drift, capacity, cost, and placement statements remain requirement- and evidence-dependent.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: The chapter does not present namespace, node, cluster, or account choice as a universal isolation theorem.

evidence: The executable boundary audit is explicitly synthetic and disclaims live cloud or Kubernetes isolation proof.
Current official guidance is attributed and retrieval-dated; provider examples are presented as implementation-specific guidance.
Production claims require effective-permission inventory, negative tests, runtime/network probes, noisy-neighbor load, fleet freshness, fault injection, restore, migration, and decommission evidence.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No achieved isolation, compliance, SLO, fleet coverage, external review, or successful recovery is claimed.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed namespace scope/granularity, RBAC/admission, pod/runtime/node controls, cluster extensions, network, cluster selection, account hierarchy, connectivity/shared services, data/keys, quota, control planes, fleets, economics, migration, and decommission.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed implementability with vendable classes, effective-permission tests, default-deny paths, runtime scheduling, organization guardrails, scoped workload identity, declarative fleet reconciliation, rollout rings, migration fencing, and independent provider cleanup.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified required section order, dense one-page review, defined notation, twelve-step boundary mechanism, sixteen trade-offs, twenty-six misconceptions, ten distinct worked examples, ten cross-program connections, fourteen references, and five progressive exercises with complete answers.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external academic or practitioner review is claimed.
